title: In re Hannaman, Glenn, Jr., Dec'd, BIIA Dec., 19 12787 (2021)
text:
Hannaman, Glenn, Jr., Dec'd
BURDEN OF PROOF
Presumption under RCW 51.32.187
In a Hanford appeal, just as in any other appeal at the Board of Industrial Insurance
Appeals, to overcome a CR 41(b)(3) motion, the party with the burden of production
must establish a prima facie case—substantial evidence which, if unrebutted, would
convince an unprejudiced, thinking mind of the truth of the issues on appeal. The Board
will follow the Morgan theory of presumptions in claims arising under RCW 51.32.187.
Accordingly, RCW 51.32.187 shifts both the burden of production and the burden of
persuasion (proof) to the employer, in this case, DOE. ....In re Glenn Hannaman Jr.,
Dec'd, BIIA Dec., 19 12787 (2021) [Editor's Note: The Board's decision was appealed to
superior court under Benton County Cause No. 21-2-01716-3]

Glenn O Hannaman, Jr., passed away from metastatic lung cancer following a 29-year career
77
with the US Department of Energy at Hanford (the "DOE"). His widow, Roberta Hannaman, filed a
88
99
beneficiary application for benefits under the Industrial Insurance Act. In a series of orders, the
1100
Department allowed the claim, denied second injury fund relief to DOE, awarded Mrs. Hannaman a
1111
1122
widow's pension, calculated Mr. Hannaman's wages, and assessed an overpayment. DOE appealed.
1133
Following a hearing, our industrial appeals judge granted the Department's CR 41 motion, and
1144
1155
dismissed the self-insured employer's appeals after determining that it failed to establish a prima facie
1166
case. DOE petitioned for review, arguing that in granting the CR 41 motion, our industrial appeals
1177
1188
judge misapplied the "clear and convincing" burden set forth in RCW 51.32.187. We agree, and grant
1199
review to reverse the CR 41 ruling. Moreover, because the parties completed their presentation of
2200
2211
evidence, we review these appeals on their merits. The uncontested record established that
2222
Mr. Hannaman was an RCW 51 covered worker on DOE related projects, within the statutorily
2233
2244
defined areas at the Hanford Nuclear Site for the requisite number of shifts. As a result, there exists
2255
a prima facie presumption that Mr. Hannaman's colorectal and lung cancers were an occupational
2266
2277
disease. Because DOE did not rebut the Hanford presumption by clear and convincing evidence,
2288
the Department Orders are AFFIRMED.
2299
3300
DISCUSSION
3311
These appeals present some procedural matters to untangle. The procedural issues may
3322
3333
have been caused by confusion regarding that legal concept known as the Burden of Proof. Black's
3344
Law Dictionary defines the term:
3355
3366
[a] party's duty to prove a disputed assertion or charge; a proposition regarding which
3377
of two contending litigants loses when there is no evidence on a question or when the
3388
answer is simply too difficult to find. The burden of proof includes both the burden of
3399
persuasion and the burden of production.1
4400
Thus, the burden of proof includes two distinct concepts. The burden of production, describes
4411
4422 one party's burden of going forward,2 that is, their burden to produce sufficient evidence to justify a
4433
4444
4455
4466 1 Black's Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019), burden of proof.
4477 2 See, Black's Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019) burden of going forward with evidence.
Page 1 of 11
11/29/21

1 finding,3 or to avoid a ruling against them (for example, summary judgment or directed verdict).4 A
2
party has met their burden of production once they have introduced sufficient evidence to establish
3
4
a prima facie case. This standard may be met even though that same evidence may fall short of
5
convincing a trier of fact to ultimately rule in the party's favor.
6
7
In contrast, the burden of persuasion is a party's duty to convince the fact-finder to view facts
8
in a way that favors that party.5 This concept assigns risk to one of the parties in the event that the
9
10
evidence is so close a fact finder cannot decide. In that instance, the party bearing the burden of
11
persuasion loses the appeal.
12
13
In most industrial insurance appeals, the appellant's burden of persuasion is by a
14
preponderance of the evidence. In criminal cases, the burden of persuasion is beyond a reasonable
15
16
doubt. In Hanford presumption cases, the burden of persuasion is clear and convincing evidence,
17
which is generally considered to be a standard in between preponderance and beyond a reasonable
18
19
doubt.
20
CR 41 Motion
21
22
Fulfilling a similar "winnowing" function as a pretrial CR 56 motion for summary judgment,
23
CR 41(b)(3) authorizes involuntary dismissal following a hearing where the moving party has failed
24
25 to meet their burden of production.6 This motion is granted when there is no evidence, or reasonable
26
inferences therefrom, which would support a verdict for the moving party. 7 Because a CR 41 motion
27
28
assesses whether a party has satisfied its burden of going forward, a CR 41(b)(3) motion to dismiss
29
amounts to an assessment of whether that party has met its burden of production.
30
31
Whose Burden is it? Application of the Morgan Theory of Presumptions
32
DOE does not dispute that Mr. Hannaman worked sufficient hours within areas covered by
33
34
RCW 51.32.187 and was subsequently diagnosed with two predicate conditions (that is, colorectal
35
and lung cancer).8 As a result, RCW 51.32.187 (the "Hanford presumption statute") establishes a
36
37
rebuttable presumption that those cancers were an occupational disease.
38
39
40
3 See, Black's Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019) burden of persuasion, second paragraph (distinguishing the two concepts
41
contained within the concept known as burden of proof.)
42 4 See, for example, Black's Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019) burden of production.
43 5 Black's Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019) burden of persuasion.
44 6 CR 41(b)(3).
45 7 See, for example, In re Donald W. Wright, Dckt. Nos. 14 16368, 14 16568, & 15 10063 (November 23, 2015) citing
Spring v. Dep't of Labor & Indus., 96 Wn.2d 914 (1982), after remand, 39 Wn. App. 751 (1985); Nelson Construction v.
46
Port of Bremerton, 20 Wn. App. 32, (1978).
47
8 Petition for Review at 17.
Page 2 of 11

1
How the Hanford presumption operates is a matter of first impression. Fortunately, we are not
2
without some direction on the topic. In 1987, our Legislature adopted a statute quite similar to the
3
4
one before us now. Amended over the years, RCW 51.32.185 (the "firefighter presumption") affords
5
certain firefighters a similar (albeit more easily disputed) presumption of occupational disease. In
6
7 Spivey v. Bellevue,9 a consolidated case involving two Bellevue firefighters diagnosed with malignant
8
melanoma, our Supreme Court clarified that in firefighter presumption cases, Washington will follow
9
10
the Morgan theory of presumptions. The Court held that employers of qualifying firefighters must
11
overcome a continuing, rather than disappearing presumption.
12
13 Noting that "RCW 51.32.185 reflects a strong social policy in favor of the worker,"10 the
14
Supreme Court concluded that whether the employer, in that case, Bellevue, rebutted the firefighter
15
16
presumption was a factual determination properly given to the jury. The court also applied the Morgan
17
theory of presumptions to RCW 51.32.185, and held that the firefighter presumption shifted both the
18
19 burden of production and the burden of persuasion to the employer.11
20
In its Petition for Review, DOE anticipates that we will follow Spivey and the Morgan Theory
21
22
of Presumptions will also be applied to RCW 51.32.187. We agree. Like the firefighter presumption,
23
the Hanford presumption statute reflects a strong social policy and must be accorded the strength
24
25
intended by our Legislature. As with the firefighter presumption, the plain language of the Hanford
26
presumption statute supports application of the Morgan theory of presumptions in these occupational
27
28
disease allowance cases. For these reasons, we hold that RCW 51.32.187 shifts both the burden of
29
production and the burden of persuasion (proof) to the employer, in this case, DOE.
30
31
Has DOE Met its Burden of Production?
32
The next issue for us to untangle is whether our industrial appeals judge properly dismissed
33
34
the self-insured employer's appeals. To overcome the Department's CR 41(b)(3) motion, DOE must
35
establish a prima facie case, that is, substantial evidence12 which, if unrebutted, would convince an
36
37 unprejudiced, thinking mind of the truth of the issues on appeal.13 Put another way, a prima facie
38
case is one that "will prevail until contradicted and overcome by other evidence."14
39
40
41
42
9 187 Wn.2d 716 (2017).
43 10 Spivey at 721.
44 11 Spivey, 187 Wn.2d 728.
45 12 A mere scintilla of evidence is insufficient. In re Peter Kim, BIIA Dec. 00 21147 at 2 (2002) citing Omeitt v. Dep't of
Labor and Indus., 21 Wn.2d 684 (1944).
46
13 In re William Morgan, Dckt. No. 91 3417 (January 14, 1993).
47
14 Black's Law Dictionary, 1189 (6th ed. 1990).
Page 3 of 11

1
Here, DOE produced medical testimony indicating that Mr. Hannaman was not exposed to
2
sufficient radiation or chemical exposures to cause his cancers. Moreover, the medical testimony
3
4
established that Mr. Hannaman's history as a smoker from 1971 to 1991 was an enormous risk factor,
5
and was most certainly the cause of his lung cancer. When considered in the light most favorable to
6
7
DOE, this unrebutted evidence is sufficient to convince an unprejudiced, thinking mind that
8
Mr. Hannaman's exposures at Hanford were not a cause of his cancers. Because our industrial
9
10
appeals judge applied a different standard to the Department's CR 41 motion (that is, DOE's clear
11
and convincing burden of persuasion), she erred in dismissing these appeals. But, our inquiry does
12
13
not end there.
14
Decision on the Merits: Clear and Convincing Evidence
15
16
Having already determined that DOE met its burden of production (that is, it established a
17
prima facie case), we next address whether it met its burden of persuasion (that is, that it rebutted
18
19
the presumption of occupational disease by clear and convincing evidence). For the reasons set
20
forth below, we find that it has not.
21
22
Black's Law Dictionary defines clear and convincing evidence as follows:
23
[e]vidence indicating that the thing to be proved is highly probable or reasonably certain.
24
This is a greater burden than preponderance of the evidence . . . but less than evidence
25
beyond a reasonable doubt, the norm for criminal trials.15
26
27 We are well acquainted with this standard of proof. Although most appeals before us are decided by
28
a preponderance of the evidence, we have long applied the higher clear and convincing standard in
29
30 willful misrepresentation cases. The Washington Pattern Jury Instructions provide:
31
A party who alleges [willful misrepresentation] [_____] has the burden of proving each
32
of the elements of [willful misrepresentation] [_____] by clear, cogent, and convincing
33
evidence.
34
35 Proof by clear, cogent, and convincing evidence means that the element must be
36 proved by evidence that carries greater weight and is more convincing than a
37 preponderance of evidence. Clear, cogent, and convincing evidence exists when
38 occurrence of the element has been shown by the evidence to be highly probable.
39 However, it does not mean that the element must be proved by evidence that is
40 convincing beyond a reasonable doubt.
41
A “preponderance of the evidence” means that you must be persuaded, considering all
42
the evidence in the case, that a proposition is more probably true than not true.
43
“Preponderance of the evidence” is defined here solely to aid you in understanding the
44
45
46
47
15 Evidence, Black's Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019). Emphasis supplied.
Page 4 of 11

1 meaning of “clear, cogent, and convincing.”16
2
Notes following this section indicate that use of WPI 160.02 is not just limited to fraud causes.
3
4 Subsequent comments indicate that although the instruction did not always include the "highly
5
probable" standard, in 2010, the WPI Committee added a sentence clarifying for jurors that "clear,
6
7 cogent, and convincing" proof means proof that an occurrence is "highly probable." Because this
8
standard is well established as a means for defining clear, cogent, and convincing evidence,17 we
9
10 apply it here.
11
DOE's Petition for Review next explores what quantum of evidence could possibly satisfy this
12
13 burden of persuasion within the unique context of RCW 51.32.187. By unique context, we refer to
14
the fact that under the Act, the distinctive conditions of employment need only be "a cause" of an
15
16 occupational disease for that condition to be covered.18
17
DOE encourages us to apply dicta from Spivey, specifically, where our Supreme Court
18
19 indicates as follows:
20
The use of the Morgan standard does not impose on the employer a burden of proving
21
the specific cause of the firefighter's melanoma. Rather, it requires that the employer
22
provide evidence from which a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that the
23
firefighter's disease was, more probably than not, caused by non-occupational factors.19
24
25 This argument misses the mark, however. Unlike the Hanford presumption statute, Spivey involved
26
a presumption statute which only obligated rebuttal proof by a preponderance of the evidence.20
27
28 Because DOE's burden of persuasion is the higher, clear and convincing standard, this dicta from
29
Spivey is inapposite.
30
31 DOE argues that the Hanford presumption statute sets an impossibly high burden for
32
employers. We disagree. The statute specifically provides that employers like DOE may successfully
33
34 rebut their presumption with evidence which "may include, but is not limited to, use of tobacco
35
products, physical fitness and weight, lifestyle, hereditary factors, and exposure from other
36
37 employment or nonemployment activities."21 As the party most able to monitor employee exposure
38
to the chemicals it asked employees to work with, and the party most able to retain those records for
39
40
41
16 WPI 160.02 (emphasis supplied).
42
17 See, for example, Dalton v. State, 130 Wn.App. 653 (2005); State Farm Fire & Cas. Co. v. Huynh, 92 Wn.App. 454,
43 465–66 (1998); see generally DeWolf & Allen, 16A Washington Practice, Tort Law & Practice § 19.2 (4th ed.); Tegland,
44 5 Washington Practice, Evidence Law and Practice § 301.3 (6th ed.).
45 18 In re Shauna Guyman, BIIA Dec., 05 13662 (2006).
19 Spivey 187 Wn.2d 716, 735 (2017), citing RCW 51.32.185(1).

1
later use, DOE can also meet its higher burden of persuasion by creating, maintaining, and producing
2
records which demonstrate that its employees are not exposed to hazardous substances in sufficient
3
4
quantities to result in conditions covered by the Hanford presumption statute.
5
DOE's Petition for Review explores a number of methods by which it could rebut the Hanford
6
7
presumption. For example, it argues it could utilize employee monitoring records to demonstrate
8
Mr. Hannaman's exposures at Hanford were insufficient to constitute a cause of his cancers. DOE
9
10
argues it could use surrogate measures of exposure and causative effect, such as comparing the
11
period between Mr. Hannaman's exposures and his cancer onset to that cancer's common latency
12
13
period. Finally, DOE suggests it could argue that the chemicals found at Hanford do not cause the
14
decedent's specific type of cancer.
15
16
Except for the last suggestion, which Division Two recently rejected in Bradley v. City of
17
Olympia,22 the remaining arguments might be an acceptable means of rebutting the Hanford
18
19
presumption assuming the right foundation. On the record before us, DOE has not carried its burden.
20
In this respect, we endorse our industrial appeals judge's factual analysis.
21
22
Factual Analysis
23
Addressing DOE's second argument next, to rely on an average latency period is to inherently
24
25
admit that within the range of acceptable latencies are latencies lower and higher than that average.
26
Moreover, averages are less helpful in situations where (as here) a claimant's exposures spanned
27
28
almost three decades.
29
Stronger was radiology and nuclear medicine specialist Fred M. Mettler, Jr., M.D.'s testimony
30
31
that the claimant's low dosimeter readings did not correlate with his rectal or lung cancers. But,
32
Dr. Mettler ignores the gaps in radiation exposure documentation, (established by certified industrial
33
34
hygienist Bruce Miller and toxicologist Joyce Tsuji, PhD) during periods when Mr. Hannaman was
35
potentially exposed to radioactive materials while working for DOE.
36
37
Dr. Mettler's opinion that Mr. Hannaman's metastatic squamous cell lung cancer was more
38
likely due to smoking and radon is likewise unpersuasive. First, Dr. Mettler conceded
39
40
Mr. Hannaman's risk of squamous cell carcinoma was really only 5.5 percent higher than a
41
nonsmoker's risk because he stopped smoking more than 25 years before his cancer diagnosis.
42
43
44
45
22 Division II, 54981-6-II (November 9, 2021) (holding that because the Legislature has already determined firefighting
46
contributes to bladder cancer, the employer must present sufficient evidence that the individual claimant's bladder cancer
47
was caused by non-occupational factors if the employer is to avoid summary judgment.)

1
Dr. Mettler also testified that welders have a 43 percent increase in lung cancer. Dr. Tsjui
2
explained that Mr. Hannaman's welding work at Hanford would have exposed him to carcinogenic
3
4
metals, particular fume and combustion products. She noted that welders commonly suffer from
5
squamous cell carcinoma—the lung cancer which spread to Mr. Hannaman's brain and ultimately
6
7
killed him. Mr. Wachtel established that Mr. Hannaman's duties at Hanford included welding.
8
Dr. Mettler's opinions also failed to consider Mr. Hannaman's occupational exposure to
9
10
carcinogenic chemicals, heavy metals, vapors and fumes (established by Mr. Miller, Dr. Tsuji,
11
Mr. Hannaman's friend and former colleague, Mark Wachtel, and family medicine specialist
12
13 Dr. Matthew Lawrence). According to Mr. Miller, chemicals23 were also openly vented from repository
14
tanks and were subject to prevailing winds around the nuclear reservation. Dr. Lawrence explained
15
16
how Mr. Hannaman's ingestion of carcinogenic chemicals (for example, inhaled plutonium particles
17
[not easily detectable by dosimeters but found in seven of Mr. Hannaman's urine samples between
18
19
1985 and 1987) increased his risk of lung cancer.
20
Although industrial hygienist Lawrence D. Yearsley felt it unlikely that Mr. Hannaman's job as
21
22
a stationary operating engineer exposed him to hazards, Mr. Miller established that the job analyses
23
upon which Mr. Yearsley relied did not likely include all the chemicals to which Mr. Hannaman was
24
25
exposed while working at Hanford. For example, some of the ventilation systems that Mr. Hannaman
26
maintained were situated in laboratory facilities where Hanford employees conducted experiments
27
28
involving many different types of fuels and waste. Without records of those experiments, no claimant
29
in Mr. Hannaman's position could quantify those exposures.
30
31
Similarly, internal medicine and medical oncologist Robert M. Levenson, M.D., concluded that
32
Mr. Hannaman's lung cancer was not caused by vapor exposure because there were no records of
33
34
chemical exposures. But, until 1987 the DOE's primary focus was weapon material production.
35
Moreover, Mr. Miller testified that no industrial hygienist program even existed in the 1980s and 1990s
36
37 (either with DOE or with its contractors).24 Given those factors, we cannot conclude that a lack of
38
documentation amounts to a lack of exposure.
39
40
41
42
43 23 Mr. Miller testified that even today the waste within these tanks has not been completely characterized.
44 24 From 2004 to 2013, Mr. Miller served as Health and Safety Director for North Wind, an environmental contractor for
45 Department of Energy. Mr. Miller testified that once industrial hygiene programs were set up, they weren't necessarily
using feedback from worker exposures to determine what types of exams and tests should be performed like modern
46
occupational medicine programs do. Instead, they were geared toward making sure workers could perform their essential
47
job functions.

1
Rather, we credit attending physician Matthew Lawrence's testimony that his patient's
2
exposures at Hanford cannot be ruled out as a cause of Mr. Hannaman's cancers. Attending
3
4
Hematologist and Oncologist Rangaswamy A. Chintapatla, M.D., agreed. Despite the stellar
5
credentials of the employer's witnesses, there is no evidence that any of them ever personally
6
7
examined Mr. Hannaman. On the other hand, physicians who attend to a claimant for a considerable
8
period are entitled to special consideration.25 This is especially the case where causation opinions
9
10
(like Dr. Lawrence's observations regarding the uncommon confluence of three rare diseases) are
11
not based solely on their patient's history of the injury.26
12
13
Given the gaps in documentation of exposure to radiation, chemicals, and vapors, the length
14
of time since Mr. Hannaman had quit smoking, and again, his uncommon confluence of rare diseases,
15
16
DOE has failed to establish, by clear and convincing evidence, that the distinctive conditions of
17
Mr. Hannaman's employment at Hanford were not a cause of his rectal and squamous cell lung
18
19
cancers.
20
The employer also appealed an order denying second injury fund relief, an order awarding a
21

beneficiary pension to Mrs. Hannaman, a bond order, and a wage order. Beyond the causation
23
arguments outlined above, which we have now addressed, DOE produced no evidence that these
24
25
orders were incorrect. The orders are likewise affirmed.

court: Washington State Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals
citation: In re Hannaman, Glenn, Jr., Dec'd, BIIA Dec., 19 12787 (2021)
subjects: BURDEN OF PROOF — Presumption under RCW 51.32.187
headnote: In a Hanford appeal, just as in any other appeal at the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals, to overcome a CR 41(b)(3) motion, the party with the burden of production must establish a prima facie case-substantial evidence which, if unrebutted, would convince an unprejudiced, thinking mind of the truth of the issues on appeal. The Board will follow the Morgan theory of presumptions in claims arising under RCW 51.32.187. Accordingly, RCW 51.32.187 shifts both the burden of production and the burden of persuasion (proof) to the employer, in this case, DOE.
